ul.li: Rio Grande do Sul: the very bottom of Brazil, next door to Uruguay and Argentina
Grassy plains, huge cattle herds, cowboys called gaúchos
The capital, Rio de Janeiro, was about 2,000 km away — weeks by horse

card.p: Simple, friendly map: Brazil's outline, the southern province shaded, Rio de Janeiro pinned far to the north.

ul.li: Charque = beef dried with salt so it keeps for months. The south's biggest product
The emperor's government taxed gaúcho charque heavily — and taxed the salt needed to make it
Charque from Uruguay and Argentina was barely taxed, so it arrived cheaper

card.p: Everyday objects on screen: a strip of dried beef, a scoop of salt, a coin.

ul.li: Brazil's emperor, Pedro II, was a nine-year-old boy — grown-up regents ruled for him
Ranchers in the south said the far-off capital took their taxes and ignored their problems
They wanted provinces to decide more for themselves

card.p: Illustrated characters: a small boy on a big throne beside a tall stack of tax papers.

ul.li: Farrapo means "rag" in Portuguese. Enemies used it to mock the rebels' fringed leather clothes
The rebels liked it and wore the name proudly
In English they became "the Ragamuffins"

card.p: Like a team turning a taunt into their own chant.

ul.li: Rancher Bento Gonçalves led rebel horsemen into Porto Alegre and took the city
The empire took it back nine months later — and kept the coast for the rest of the war
So the Ragamuffins made the wide inland grasslands their home ground
After winning at Seival, they declared the Riograndense Republic on 11 September 1836
Bento Gonçalves was chosen as its first president
Its motto: Liberty, Equality, Humanity

card.p: Second simple map: the new republic outlined inside Brazil, with a small flag marker.

ol.li: 1837 — Bento Gonçalves escapes from prison and returns
1839 — Boats travel overland; Laguna falls; the Juliana Republic is born
1842 — The empire sends its best general, the Baron of Caxias

card.p: Colorful dot timeline running left to right — the deck's timeline card.

ul.li: Bento Gonçalves — cattle rancher, first president, famous prison escaper
Giuseppe Garibaldi — Italian sailor who ran the rebel navy, later a hero of Italy's unification
Anita Garibaldi — Brazilian rider and sailor who fought beside him
Antônio de Sousa Neto — the general who announced the new republic
David Canabarro — commander of the march on Laguna

card.p: Row of friendly illustrated portraits, no weapons.

card.h1: The time they put boats on wheels

ul.li: 1839: imperial warships bottled up the rebel boats inside a huge lagoon
Garibaldi's fix: lift two boats onto giant wooden carriages and roll them across land
Around 100 oxen per boat, about 100 km of fields, sand and marsh, in six days
They splashed back into water at Tramandaí — the empire never noticed

card.p: Hero illustration: a sailing boat on a cart pulled by a long line of oxen through grass.

card.h1: A second republic — for four months

ul.li: The boat trick worked: the Ragamuffins captured the port of Laguna on 22 July 1839
They declared the Juliana Republic in the neighbouring province
It lasted about four months before the empire took the port back
One of the two boats had already sunk in a storm; Garibaldi swam out alive
The rebels formed the Black Lancers — units of freed and formerly enslaved men, created from 1836
Some were promised their freedom in exchange for fighting
But the republic's 1843 constitution kept slavery, and most rebel leaders enslaved people themselves
Many never received the freedom they were promised

card.p: Handled plainly and gently: honesty about the part of the story the hero tales leave out.

card.h1: How it ended: a deal, not a battle

ul.li: 1 March 1845: the Treaty of Ponche Verde
Everyone was pardoned, and rebel soldiers joined the imperial army
The south got to pick its next governor, and the empire paid the republic's debts
And imported charque finally got a 25% tax

card.p: So they gave up their country — but won the argument they started over.

card.h1: Why people still talk about it

ul.li: Ten years long — the biggest and longest of Brazil's regional revolts
Rio Grande do Sul still celebrates 20 September every year
Garibaldi sailed home and helped unite Italy
"Farroupilha" went from insult to badge of pride

ol.li: What food started the whole argument?
What does the word farrapo mean?
How old was Emperor Pedro II when the war began?
How did Garibaldi get his boats past the warships?
How many years did the war last?

card.p: Five playful question cards with icons — no answers on this slide.

ol.li: "Rag" — a nickname the rebels turned into a badge of honour
He rolled them overland on ox-drawn carts

brief.instruction: Write for children roughly 8–12 and the adult reading it with them. Sentence case, warm and plain, like a favourite teacher telling a story — curious, never babyish, never solemn. About 30 words per slide; the template holds median 29, p90 64, so budget 29 a slide and only approach 64 on the timeline and quiz slides, which are lists. Short sentences. Concrete nouns a child can picture: salt, coins, oxen, boats, a boy on a throne. Explain any term the moment it appears (charque, republic, regent, province). Numbers and dates stay exactly as written in the outline — they are researched facts. Vary sentence and paragraph length. No "Bold term: explanation" list formatting beyond the few lead-in labels already in the outline. No signposting ("Let's explore", "In this section"). No sweeping openers or inspirational closers. No "not just X — it's Y" constructions. No em dashes.

Bright, colorful and picture-book friendly throughout, in the template's scrapbook language: paper cards, soft organic photo masks, tilted notecards, dot timeline. Absolutely no violent battle imagery: no fighting, no weapons pointed, no blood, no corpses, no burning towns. Where the story touches conflict, show people, places, animals, objects and maps instead. Use warm, hand-drawn style illustration rather than photographs for people and scenes; this is a history no camera recorded. The deck needs these specific visual moments: - Two simple, uncluttered maps: Brazil with the southern province shaded and the far-off capital pinned; then the breakaway republic outlined. Big shapes, few labels, no dense cartography. - One clear horizontal timeline card with six dated dots (slide 8). - One illustrated character row of five friendly portraits (slide 9), no weapons. - Everyday objects as explainers: dried beef, salt, a coin, tax papers, a fringed leather poncho, a wooden cart wheel, an ox yoke. - The boats-on-oxcarts slide is the deck's showstopper: give it the biggest, most joyful illustration in the deck. - The quiz and answer slides should feel like a game show, with playful numbered chips. Keep each slide to one image idea. Faces friendly and diverse.

This is real history for children, so simplify without distorting. Do not invent dialogue, extra characters, statistics, or dramatic scenes that are not in the outline. Keep the Black Lancers slide honest and gentle: the promise of freedom, the 1843 constitution that kept slavery, the promise unkept. Do not soften it into a happy ending and do not add graphic detail. Do not describe the Ragamuffins as an anti-slavery movement; they were not. Frame the ending as a negotiated treaty, not a glorious victory or a crushing defeat.
